newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: INTERVIEW - Sri Lankan rubber exports seen plunging.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Sri Lankan rubber exports seen plunging.

text.p: Sri Lanka's rubber exports are expected to drop sharply by the year 2000 because of growing domestic demand from the local rubber-related manufacturing industry, a top rubber industry official said on Friday.
"The rubber-based industry has grown phenomenally over the last five years," William Tissa Ellawala, chairman of the Colombo Rubber Traders Association, said in an interview.
"By the year 2000 we estimate that as much as 50 percent of all rubber made in Sri Lanka will be used locally in value-added rubber based products," he said.

Raw rubber exports, Sri Lanka's biggest export commodity after tea, fell to 68.2 million kg (150.4 million lbs) in 1995 from the previous year's 69.1 million (152.3 million lbs), the government's Rubber Development Department said.
Sri Lanka's 1995 rubber production of 105.7 million kg (233 million lbs) was up only marginally from the previous year's 105.3 million kg (232.1 million lbs).

But earnings from rubber rose to a stunning 5.7 billion rupees ($100 million) last year from 1994's 3.6 billion rupees due to record world prices, which industry analysts attribute to higher world demand as economies emerge from recession coupled with a shortage in producer nations which had cut back production when prices were low.
The breakup of the Soviet Union, the world's biggest producer, also led to a sharp fall in synthetic rubber output.
Sri Lanka currently produces only two percent of the world's rubber and is ranked the eighth largest producer in the world, down from the fourth largest in 1980.
Domestic consumption was growing with new glove, tyre and other rubber-based industries being set up, said Ellawala whose association groups rubber growers, exporters and brokers.

Ellawala said 10 years ago only 15 percent of domestically produced rubber was used in the local industry. "By 1992 we used 28 percent in local rubber-based industry and last year the figure was 38 percent," he added.
Exporters said production this year was expected to be around the same as 1995 because rain has affected tapping despite efforts to increase the use of rainguards.
Rubber output by the year 2000 is estimated to be around 123-126 million kg (271-278 million lbs). Production was a record 155 million kg (342 million lbs) in 1978.
The country produces only two percent of the world's rubber and is now ranked the eighth-biggest producer in the world, down from the fourth-biggest in 1980.

Ellawala said output had fallen sharply in the last 10 years mainly because producers abandoned rubber land after years of poor prices. Land was re-developed for industrial expansion and village resettlement and producers faced a lack of tappers.
Also a large amount of old rubber land has been replanted, he said. "Trees take six years to mature to give latex."
The Rubber Development Department said the rubber area had fallen to around 161,479 hectares (399,019 acres) from 171,152 hectares (422,921 acres) in the early 1980s.
But production is expected to recover because of the accelerated replanting programme and increasing use of high-yielding clones, Ellawala said.
